fidelity: (a) |dv/dt|=|a| is the magnitude of the acceleration: the total rate of change of the velocity vector, including both change in speed and change in direction. d|v|/dt is the rate of change of speed only; it is the tangential component of acceleration (positive when speeding up, negative when slowing down). (b) Yes. Using a_t=d|v|/dt and a_n=v²/R, |dv/dt|=sqrt(a_t²+a_n²). Hence |dv/dt|=d|v|/dt iff a_n=0 and d|v|/dt>=0, i.e. v×a=0 and v·a>=0: acceleration is along the velocity or zero. In simple NCERT terms, this occurs in straight-line motion with non-decreasing speed; if speed is constant, both are zero only when acceleration is zero. If a straight-line motion is slowing down, |dv/dt|=-d|v|/dt, so as written they are not equal unless signs/magnitudes are ignored.
